html:
I like the idea that “the brain counts the frequency of the sound.” It’s crude, but it isn’t wrong.

In terms of anatomy, the ear has three main parts: the outer ear, the tympanic cavity and the inner ear (1, 2 and 3 in the figure below).

In terms of signal conversion, sound goes through the following stages before the brain perceives it: mechanical vibration, then neural electrical signals, then central processing.

In terms of mechanical sound propagation, sound travels in turn through air, through solid structures and through fluid.

Hearing a sound is no small feat.

1. The outer ear

The outer ear consists of the pinna, the ear canal and the eardrum.

  • The pinna plays an important role in spatial hearing. For example, close your eyes and have a high-frequency sound played first in front of you and then behind you. Because of the peculiar shape of the pinna, the sound reflects off it differently in each case, so the sound reaching the inner ear is different, and that is how we can tell whether it is in front or behind. This is called a spectral cue. Of course, it only works for high-frequency sounds. At low frequencies the wavelength is so long that, with our eyes closed, we find it hard to tell front from back.

Someone on YouTube did a delightful experiment: he blindfolded his son and clapped his hands at different spots around him, and the boy always pointed in the right direction. Then he stuck modeling clay onto the boy’s pinnae, and the boy was completely lost.

  • The ear canal joins the pinna at its outer end and ends at the eardrum. In adults it is on average 2.7 cm long and 6–8 mm in diameter. It behaves like a quarter-wave resonator with a resonance around 3 kHz, which is also where the ear is most sensitive. For sounds with f > 3 kHz, the ear canal acts as an amplifier.
  • The eardrum (tympanic membrane) is like the diaphragm of a loudspeaker, only much smaller: just 85 mm², with an effective area of no more than 55 mm², and about 0.1 mm thick. Sound collected by the outer ear sets the eardrum vibrating, and the vibration passes on to the next stage: the tympanic cavity.

2. The tympanic cavity

The tympanic cavity is filled with air and connected to the Eustachian tube, which equalizes it with the atmospheric pressure outside. Running from the eardrum across the cavity are three small bones, the ossicles, linked in sequence: the malleus, the incus and the stapes. They pass the sound on to the oval window and from there to the cochlea in the inner ear.

The stapes is attached to the stapedius muscle, which acts as a kind of “fuse.” When incoming sound exceeds 85 dB HL (HL stands for hearing level: the sound pressure level corrected for the sensitivity of individual hearing), this muscle protects the inner ear by holding back the motion.

In the figure below you can see that the eardrum, the three ossicles and the oval window get smaller and smaller. Why? Because the cochlea contains not air but lymph fluid. If the tympanic cavity were connected directly to the cochlea, the human world would be silent: with the much higher impedance, and with too little pressure from the vibrating eardrum, sound would be almost entirely reflected! The chain of eardrum, malleus, incus, stapes and oval window amplifies the pressure so that the sound can make it to the final stage. This is called impedance matching.

Besides the route through the tympanic cavity, sound can reach the inner ear another way: bone conduction. The simplest demonstration: cover your ears (assuming we have giant, all-powerful hands), and you can still hear yourself talk. Sounds muffled, doesn’t it? That is because hearing through bone conduction is far less sensitive than hearing through the ear canal.

3. The inner ear

If the auditory system were a person, the inner ear would be its brain. This is where sound is converted into electrochemical signals, which the central auditory system then processes, analyzes and perceives.

The structure of the inner ear, and of the cochlea in particular, leaves me in awe: humans really are the most precise machines on this planet.

The stapes connects to the bony labyrinth, which is filled with lymph fluid. The snail on the far right →_→ is the cochlea. Uncoiled, this snail is about 30–35 mm long, with a diameter of 0.3–0.9 mm. In the cochlea, sound undergoes a change of state: at last, the mechanical signal becomes an electrical one. Put simply, this is the path sound takes through the cochlea:

— Sound enters through the chamber above the basilar membrane and leaves through the chamber below it, setting the basilar membrane vibrating

— The stereocilia on the hair cells detect the vibration and convert it into electrical signals

— The electrical signals travel along axons to the brain for processing

— Huh, did I just hear something?

The organ of Corti carries nearly 20,000 hair cells, and each hair cell has 50–150 stereocilia. (If you have trypophobia, best not to think about it too hard: there is a monster like this living in your ear.)

Another awesome trick of the cochlea is its “Fourier transform”: different places pick up different frequencies.

Toward the outside of the cochlea, the basilar membrane is stiffer, so only high frequencies can set this part vibrating and be sensed by its hair cells. Toward the inside, it is the opposite: the membrane is less stiff, so the hair cells there mainly detect low frequencies. Loudspeakers work the same way: subwoofers tend to be big, with low stiffness, while tweeters are much smaller and stiffer. That is how we can tell sounds of different frequencies apart: a bass sounds deeper than a guitar, women’s voices are higher than men’s, and so on.

What’s more, within the same space, a coiled cochlea can pick up lower frequencies than a straight one would, which is what lets us hear down to 20 Hz.

A digression: I can’t resist a word on how transparent Chinese words are.
耳蜗 (ěrwō, cochlea) = the organ inside the ear (耳, ěr) that looks like a snail (蜗牛, wōniú)
cochlea = ??
I only found out by looking it up: it was borrowed from the Greek κοχλίας (kōhlias), literally “spiral snail shape.” For so many words, English simply imports foreign terms wholesale, without a shred of originality…
When it comes to transparent words, German is every bit as good as Chinese: Hörschnecke. Hör- comes from hören (to hear), and Schnecke = snail.

With all that said, back to the original question:

When we hear a note, we perceive a pitch. How exactly does this happen in the brain?

Answered.

People online say the brain counts the frequency of the sound, but I don’t think that’s quite right. First, how could it possibly keep count of the thousands, even tens of thousands, of vibrations per second in a high-frequency sound?

It can keep count, just not with the brain. The brain has more important things to do; this kind of grunt work can be left to the basilar membrane and the hair cells.

Second, I tested myself today and found that, without distractions, I can tell apart two tones near 440 Hz that differ by 0.4 Hz. Wouldn’t the brain miscount a difference that small?

The book Psychoacoustics tells us [4]:

Below 500 Hz, the ear can distinguish pure tones 1 Hz apart. Above 500 Hz, this threshold (technically the just-noticeable frequency difference, or JNFD) is 0.002 × the frequency. At 1000 Hz, for example, we can hear a difference of 2 Hz. These are averages, though. Our questioner probably has an unusually finely graded stiffness gradient along the basilar membrane, plus a few extra hair cells ;)

I finished this answer just before the end of 2018. Happy New Year 2019, everyone!
